segments.title: Why historians seek unusual practical experiences
segments.summary: Historians cannot recreate much of the past, so varied present-day experience can offer limited points of comparison.
segments.body: Many conditions from the past cannot be recreated. Present-day experience can still offer relative points of comparison when thinking about historical work and choices. Those comparisons have limits because modern circumstances differ from the past. Their value lies in making otherwise abstract demands easier to imagine.
segments.question: Why do naval historians and historians in general so often seem like 'nutty professors' willing to try unusual things?
segments.answerShort: Because much of the past cannot be recreated, historians seek varied present-day experiences that provide relative comparisons.

evidence.note: He says many features of the past cannot be recreated and that current experience supplies relative points of comparison.

segments.title: What building work reveals about shipyards and dry docks
segments.summary: House repairs provide a limited comparison for the teamwork, physical effort, and weather exposure involved in building shipyards and dry docks.
segments.body: Recent roof, heating, plumbing, and carpentry work provides a limited comparison for historical construction. Building shipyards, dry docks, and related facilities was a different undertaking, yet both depend on teamwork and sustained physical effort. Weather also changes the character of outdoor work. A Cornish winter requires scaffolding and shelter, while summer allows much more freedom of movement. The comparison gives some practical sense of the labour behind naval infrastructure without treating house repairs as equivalent to industrial construction.

evidence.note: He describes roof, heating, plumbing, and carpentry work before linking that experience to shipyards, dry docks, teamwork, effort, and winter outdoor conditions.
